title: Comparative Evaluation of Explainable AI Techniques for Histopathology-Based Cancer Detection Using Deep Learning
abstract: The analysis of histopathological images is an important method of diagnosing cancer. Deep learning models, such as convolutional neural networks and transformer-based models have demonstrated great potential in automated cancer detection. However, they are black-box and cannot be understood in a clinical context. In this paper, a comparative study is conducted to analyze the explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) approaches for cancer detection based on histopathology images on a hybrid model based on deep learning networks: ResNet-18 and Vision Transformer (ViT). The hybrid model is trained on histopathology images and three explainability mechanisms are used, including Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, and Score-CAM to visualize regions of decisions made. The created heatmaps are evaluated according to the accuracy of localization, noise minimization, and interpretability. Experimental results indicate that Grad-CAM++ provides better localization and Score-CAM generates more smooth and noisy explanations. This comparative analysis enhances transparency of models and helps to make more credible medical decisions.

title: Cauchy distribution optimizer with neighborhood search for PV parameter estimation and numerical optimization
abstract: This paper proposes an enhanced version of the Cauchy Distribution Optimizer (CDO) integrated with a Neighborhood Search (NS) mechanism for solving numerical optimization problems and extracting parameters of photovoltaic (PV) models. The original CDO, inspired by the Cauchy probability distribution, demonstrates competitive performance in balancing exploration and exploitation. However, like many metaheuristic algorithms, it may suffer from premature convergence and insufficient local search capability when handling complex multimodal problems. To address these limitations, we introduce a Neighborhood Search strategy that performs refined local exploration around promising solutions, thereby improving solution accuracy and convergence reliability. The proposed CDO-NS algorithm is validated using three PV models (Single Diode Model, Double Diode Model, and Photovoltaic Module Model). Experimental results demonstrate that CDO-NS outperforms the original CDO and other state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of solution quality, convergence speed, and statistical significance. The source code of CDO-NS(referred to as NSCDO throughout the paper) is made publicly available for further research.

title: An Intelligent Quality Assurance Pipeline for Large-Scale Personal Dosimetry Services Using Unsupervised Machine Learning-Based Anomaly Detection on Multi-Element TLD Readouts
abstract: Large-scale national personal dosimetry programs require stringent data quality assurance (QA) to prevent false exposure reports. Traditional QA relies on manual review or scalar thresholds, which fail to detect multi-dimensional anomalies. This paper presents an intelligent QA pipeline evaluating six unsupervised machine learning models against physics-grounded reference labels. We compiled a unified dataset of 14,732 records by programmatically matching raw reader outputs with dose spreadsheets (2024–2026), recovering 8,487 missing barcodes at a 99.1% matching rate via floating-point response fingerprinting. Evaluation against 379 physical anomalies proved that Isolation Forest achieved the highest performance (F1 = 0.580 at 1.5% contamination; F1 = 0.743 and Recall = 0.744 at 2.85% contamination), significantly outperforming One-Class SVM, Local Outlier Factor, and Elliptic Envelope (pairwise McNemar's tests with continuity correction, p < 0.001). Feature ablation confirmed that combining element shares, ratios, and operational metrics maximizes detection for Isolation Forest, while sensitivity analysis proved stable performance. The consensus intersection model yielded an operational precision of 0.592. This pipeline demonstrates the feasibility of integrating unsupervised learning into routine radiation protection workflows to safeguard national occupational dose registries.

title: AiSearch: Interactive Multi-Modal Search with VLMs
abstract: Modern retrieval systems must both be automated and interactive, allowing users to search and refine results in real time. We present AiSearch, a flexible multimodal retrieval framework that leverages the zero shot capabilities of Vision Language Models (VLMs) for natural language search over images and videos. AiSearch supports interactive search refinement through user feedback to tailor results to the user's intent, and allows visual benchmarking across multiple VLMs, enabling users to select the most suitable model for their task.

title: Augmenting Rewrite Rule Sets via Knuth-Bendix Completion
abstract: Equality Saturation (EqSat) is a powerful technique for program optimization, systematically exploring the search space of candidate programs to overcome the phase ordering problem. However, the feasibility and performance of EqSat rely heavily on the specific rewrite rules used to derive equivalent programs. These rule sets are typically handcrafted, requiring extensive domain expertise and carrying the risk of missing valuable transformations. In this work, we evaluate Knuth-Bendix Completion (KBC) as a method for automatically generating and augmenting rewrite rules for EqSat. Our experiments show faster optimization as well as reaching better terms with previously missed optimizations.

title: Synthesis of Compact and Expressive Quantum-Circuit Optimizations
abstract: Today’s quantum devices are noisy, so reducing circuit size is critical for reliable execution. Existing rule-based optimizers often rely on large rule sets that are difficult to manage and still miss long-distance transformations. We present QSymb, a framework for synthesizing compact and expressive quantum-circuit rewrite rules with formal guarantees. We formalize symbolic rewrite rules in which a symbolic gate represents infinitely many subcircuits. We then define canonical symbolic rules of the form L ; S = S ; R and prove that they constitute a compact generative core from which general symbolic rules can be derived. On top of this formal foundation, given a gate set, QSymb synthesizes (1) a small, non-derivable concrete rule set that is complete up to chosen size and qubit bounds, and (2) a small but expressive canonical symbolic rule set that captures transformations beyond finite or monomial-only patterns. We further present rule anchoring to derive optimization-effective rules from canonical symbolic rules. Together, these results provide both expressiveness and guarantees: soundness of synthesized rules via validation, non-derivability, and bounded completeness. On the IBM-Eagle gate set, QSymb strictly outperforms state-of-the-art rewrite-based optimizers (Qiskit, Guoq, Quartz, TKET, and Queso) in two-qubit-gate reduction on 90%, 67%, 82%, 85%, and 83% of standard quantum algorithm benchmarks, respectively; on Nam gate set, the corresponding rates are 88%, 74%, 81%, 86%, and 82.9%. It achieves final average two-qubit-gate reductions of 27.44% and 29.95%, respectively.

title: Semantic model for the SKA Regional Centre Network
abstract: The sheer magnitude of data to be collected by the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) telescopes necessitates robust and dependable strategies for the effective management and processing of data. In this context, the SKA Regional Centre Network (SRCNet), a collaborative global infrastructure comprising multiple regional centres distributed worldwide, is expected to play a central role in handling and analysing the extensive data streams generated by the telescopes, thereby enabling significant advances in astronomical research and exploration. This paper introduces a semantic model for the SRCNet that is sufficiently detailed to describe its architecture, data distribution, and computing services. By explicitly defining nodes, resources, relationships, and workflows, the model provides a foundation for interoperability and efficient resource management within the distributed network. The model supports two configurations, centralised and decentralised, depending on the location of data storage. In future deployments, a service broker will be able to plan workflows efficiently by querying nodes for real-time system availability. To validate and assess the integrity of the model, consistency tests are conducted using SPARQL queries. This work advances semantic modelling in astronomy by presenting, for the first time, a semantic model tailored to the SRCNet. The proposed model serves as a precursor to a more formal mathematical representation of the network and establishes a foundational framework for the development of a future service broker.

title: Dynamic Cognitive Gating: Separating Epistemic Rigor from Interaction Style in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models trained on human preferences tend to agree with their users rather than evaluate them, a failure known as sycophancy. We argue that a structural cause has been overlooked: a single behavioural policy is asked to serve brainstorming, critique and factual checking at once, and preference training settles on a compromise that is wrong for each. Dynamic Cognitive Gating (DCGN) separates these functions explicitly. Interaction modes form a rigor-ordered space, from free-wheeling articulation to strict claim-level verification, selected per turn by a learned gating policy. Crucially, a mode-blind verification floor guarantees that every material error the verifier detects is disclosed in every mode: style adapts freely, and disclosure cannot be switched off. Completeness is bounded by the verifier's recall, which the design measures separately and protects with verifier diversity, tool-grounded checks and thresholds calibrated by conformal risk control. The design also separates two learning problems usually conflated, what each mode looks like and when to use it, correcting the shared bias in user labels with group-conditional transition matrices estimated from independent relabelling. An asymmetric switching rule prevents the system from autonomously lowering rigor below the audit level on factual content. Clarification queries are issued only where ambiguity changes whether full critique is rendered, or where a material error appears in a permissive mode. The paper is a specification with falsifiable hypotheses, a preregistrable evaluation protocol, an embedded prototype specification and an explicit list of open problems; no empirical results are reported.

title: CapOpt: Capability-Aware Superoptimization for Secure and Provably Faster Code
abstract: Superoptimization is a powerful code optimization technique that generates optimized instruction sequences by exploring the space of instruction-level transformations. However, existing superoptimizers assume that pointers and integers are interchangeable, an assumption that no longer holds in memory-security-enhanced architectures like CHERI, where pointers are represented as metadata-rich capabilities with enforced bounds, permissions, and provenance. This semantic change breaks many traditional optimizations and forces CHERI compilers to adopt conservative strategies that sacrifice performance for safety. We present CapOpt, the first superoptimization framework that explicitly incorporates capability semantics into both its search space and correctness model. CapOpt introduces Provenance-Guided Stratified Synthesis (PGSS), a synthesis strategy that structures the search space around capability-aware abstractions and uses provenance-based reasoning to eliminate unsafe transformations. We also define a capability-aware equivalence model that extends conventional functional correctness to include metadata integrity. We evaluated CapOpt on an ARM-based CHERI hardware platform and the CHERI-RISC-V simulator. Experimental results show that CapOpt improves performance by up to 4.1% over the existing CHERI-LLVM toolchain, while strengthening security by tightening pointer bounds and permissions.

title: Towards Concise Binding Semantics of Late-Bound OOP Systems
abstract: Smalltalk and Self are two paradigmatic examples of class-based and prototype-based late-bound object-oriented programming, respectively. Many of their similarities and differences can be grounded in how they bind message names to concrete values, but the details can be subtle and are not available in a concise form. The Id object model abstracts over specific binding semantics, even permitting the flexibility of late-bound message sending as part of binding semantics, so it is worth using as a common basis on which to compare them. In this paper, we present the method-binding semantics of Smalltalk and Self as different “special cases” within the Id object model.

title: Datura: Progressive Red Teaming Testing for Tool Invocation Chain in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents that invoke external tools face critical safety vulnerabilities when malicious manipulations exploit their implicit trust in tool outputs and metadata. However, identifying these vulnerabilities through testing is challenging due to the need to bypass safety guardrails with semantically legitimate inputs, the difficulty in characterizing successful attacks amid implicit tool trust, and the requirement to maintain logical consistency across fragile state-dependent execution chains. In this paper, we first conduct an empirical study to investigate how external tools influence agent reasoning. Guided by the findings, we propose Datura, an automated red teaming testing framework that exposes safety vulnerabilities through chained tool manipulation. Through a five-stage workflow, Datura dynamically generates test cases where each individual step appears legitimate yet collectively leads to harmful outcomes. We evaluate Datura across five LLMs and 740 safety-critical tasks under five defense settings, including real-world safety mechanisms. Under Model Alignment, Datura achieves 94.86--99.59% attack success rate (ASR), outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 25.27 percentage points. Under Prompt Refuge, Datura maintains 78.78--95.54% ASR, showing that progressive tool-chain manipulation remains effective even under prompt-level safeguards.

title: A Multi‐Region Deep Learning Framework for Low‐Frequency Earthquake Detection: Application to the Guerrero Seismic Gap
abstract: Abstract Low‐frequency earthquakes (LFEs) provide key constraints on slow earthquake processes but remain difficult to detect because of their low signal‐to‐noise ratios (SNR) and emergent onsets, particularly in offshore environments where seismic networks are sparse. In this study, we develop a deep learning framework for LFE detection trained on a curated multi‐region data set spanning six tectonic environments. To address uncertainties in arrival timing and improve robustness to noisy waveforms, we employ probabilistic Gaussian labels and incorporate multi‐station waveform inputs within a modified U‐Net architecture. The model demonstrates stable training convergence and consistent detection performance on an independent held out test set containing previously unused events from multiple regions. We apply the trained model to continuous ocean‐bottom seismometer (OBS) data in the Guerrero seismic gap in Mexico. After target‐domain threshold calibration, the workflow recovered 21 events from an existing catalog and identified 25 additional offshore LFE candidates. These detections show temporal clustering and a spatial distribution that differed partly from that of the existing catalog. Our results suggest that deep learning may complement matched‐filter detection in regions where template libraries or offshore observations are limited.

title: Taxiway path planning in airports based on Elite-guided Dynamic Lévy-flight Particle Swarm Optimization
abstract: Airport taxiway path planning is crucial to airport surface operations but involves complex taxiway networks, temporal separation requirements, and potential taxiing conflicts. Standard PSO and conventional variants often suffer from premature convergence, insufficient population diversity, and limited adaptability to constrained and discrete search spaces. To address these limitations, an Elite-guided Dynamic Lévy-flight Particle Swarm Optimization algorithm (EDL-PSO) is developed to solve the airport taxiway path planning problem. The EDL-PSO integrates fitness-driven momentum adjustment, diversity-enhanced perturbation, and elite-guided redistribution. A dynamic inertia weight strategy adjusts particle momentum according to population fitness improvement to balance global exploration and local exploitation. Meanwhile, a diversity-triggered Lévy-flight mutation strategy introduces long-range perturbations to recover exploratory capability under population concentration. Furthermore, an elite-guided restart strategy reinitializes non-elite particles around high-quality solutions while preserving useful search information under persistent stagnation. Experiments are conducted on the CEC 2017 benchmark suite and real airport scenarios. The EDL-PSO achieves the best overall ranking among the state-of-the-art algorithms on the CEC 2017 benchmark suite, with superiority confirmed by statistical analysis. In the representative real airport scenario, the average taxiing time is reduced to 151.84, with a best result of 145.63 and a standard deviation of 2.85. Compared with ESD-PSO, which obtains the lowest average taxiing time among the comparison PSO variants, the EDL-PSO reduces the average taxiing time by approximately 11.7%, demonstrating the effectiveness and stability under realistic airport surface operations. The proposed conflict-aware metaheuristic method can be applied to support taxiway path planning and conflict avoidance.

title: A meta-learning with adversarial domain adaptation method for few-shot cross-region maize height and yield joint prediction
abstract: High accuracy phenotypic prediction driven by genotype (G), environment (E) and their interactions is the foundation for precision crop breeding. However, under cross-region few-shot scenarios with domain shift, prediction accuracy and model generalization are often declined. To address this challenge, a novel phenotype prediction framework, namely Meta-learning with Adversarial domain adaptation for G × E Prediction (MAGEP), is established. The framework first introduces a GEfused module with a dual-branch architecture to extract fused genotypic and environmental features. It then employs Reptile-based meta-learning to learn generalizable features across environments. A gradient reversal layer is incorporated to perform adversarial training for learning domain-invariant features. Meanwhile, Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) or Correlation Alignment (CORAL) domain alignment strategies are applied to quantify and reduce the feature distribution discrepancy between source and target domains. Using a publicly available maize G × E dataset, the MAGEP was compared with eleven baseline models in four cross-domain prediction scenarios. The results show that MAGEP outperforms all baselines in both accuracy and robustness. Notably, MAGEP_CORAL achieves the best performance, reaching average Pearson correlation coefficients (PCC) of 0.75 for plant height and 0.45 for grain yield, improvements of 44.2% and 55.2% over MAGEP_MMD, respectively. Experiments with varying target-domain sample sizes further confirm the superior adaptability of the CORAL strategy. Furthermore, cross-year and cross-species experiments confirm that MAGEP achieved lower RMSE and MAE than baseline models. Finally, post-hoc interpretability analysis was performed on MAGEP using gradient-based attribution methods. The findings reveal that plant height and grain yield are regulated by multiple genetic loci, and the model can identify key environmental regulators for each trial locations. This supports the biological plausibility of MAGEP model and provide a basis for analyzing the genetic and environmental co-regulation of crop phenotypes.

title: Simulation-based validation of multivariate time-series anomaly detection algorithms for aircraft edge systems
abstract: This study presents a systematic approach for selecting and evaluating anomaly detection algorithms for the development of an edge system for real-time aircraft data analysis. Using the HAI 21.03 dataset, a highly imbalanced dataset in which anomalies account for less than 3% of the total data, the performance of a prediction-based Long Short-Term Memory Prediction (LSTM Pred) model and reconstruction-based Long Short-Term Memory Autoencoder (LSTM AE), Convolutional Neural Network–Long Short-Term Memory Autoencoder (CNN–LSTM AE), Variational Autoencoder (VAE), and Transformer-based anomaly detection (TransAD) models is compared. Based on the analysis of real-time processing capability and the F1-score, the LSTM AE model is selected for further evaluation. Normal and abnormal flight operation simulation data are generated using the commercial flight simulation software X-Plane. When abnormal data are input into the selected LSTM AE model, increased Mean Squared Error (MSE) values are observed near the injected fault events. These results suggest that LSTM AE is a promising candidate for real-time anomaly detection in aircraft edge systems under the experimental conditions considered in this study.

title: AI-driven Thermal-aware Data Center Capacity Planning
abstract: The emerging of large language models (LLMs) has posed significant challenges to the thermal management of data center. Intense GPU computation for LLMs results in localized hotspots. Moreover, spiking thermal loads during training and inference bursts make real-time cooling response more difficult to predict and control. Thermal-aware capacity planning of data center requires massive expensive high-fidelity CFD simulations. AI models can perform real-time prediction for unseen designs. However, existing works either have large prediction error, or have over-simplified assumptions for data center operations. This work presents an AI-driven framework that can perform thermal-aware capacity planning for a real-world data center in seconds. The embedded AI model learns from numerous key parameters (rack power, server power, server placement, HVAC settings etc.), and provides temperature prediction within milliseconds. This AI model is tested against high-fidelity CFD simulations, and results show that for unseen data center designs, model can achieve high accuracy with 10000X speedup. Driven by the AI model, the authors design the thermal-aware capacity planning framework. This framework can help data center designers and operators instantaneously optimize both workload distribution and HVAC cooling efficiency.

title: Premonoidal Semantics and Scalable Diagrammatics of Fermionic Quantum Computing
abstract: Local fermionic mode (LFM) based quantum computation has pure state spaces that are isomorphic, via the Jordan-Wigner representation, to qubit state spaces, but its compositional structure is subtly different. Indeed, the algebraic formalism specifying how to embed fermionic systems underlies a notion of parallel composition, for which, in general, the usual interchange law of monoidal categories fails. We give a categorical account of this phenomenon. Starting from the CAR-algebraic semantics of fermionic gate application, we show that LFM processes form a symmetric premonoidal category whose centre is precisely the even, parity-preserving subcategory. The same processes can alternatively be organized with the ordinary tensor product and a fermionic presymmetry that is natural exactly on even maps. To reason diagrammatically in this latter presentation, we introduce pronaps, a relaxation of the notion of prop, in which permutations are not-necessarily-natural, and use them to organize a hierarchy of fragments of the fermionic ZW calculus relevant to the study of fermionic circuits on physically motivated gate-sets. We then extend scalable diagrammatic notation to pronaps. In this setting, syntactic sugars inspired by SZX and GSA are defined, with the specificity that matrix arrows encode minors and determinants, while graph triangles encode pfaffians of principal submatrices. These constructions yield elegant normal forms and completeness proofs for our presentations of the EoW, FoW, EW, and FW fragments. In particular, the FW presentation gives a new normal form for the matchgate fragment, distinct from the rWGS-X normal form of the planar-W (pW) presentation of the same category. The resulting framework connects fermionic circuit semantics, diagrammatic rewriting with scalable notations, and the algebra of determinants and pfaffians.

title: Muon meets Tamed Langevin: Momentum Preconditioning beyond Convex and gradient-Lipschitz Potentials
abstract: We consider the problem of sampling from Gibbs distributions on matrix spaces whose potential energies are neither convex nor globally gradient-Lipschitz. We introduce a family of non-quadratic kinetic energies that lead to a new underdamped Langevin system with momentum preconditioning, in which the gradient of the kinetic energy acts as a smooth spectral taming of the momentum. We prove that, under these relaxed assumptions on the potential, the resulting dynamics leaves the target Gibbs measure invariant, and we establish exponential convergence to equilibrium in a weighted total variation distance. Finally, we show that the corresponding Euler-Maruyama discretization admits moment bounds that are uniform in time, without any modification of the potential gradient, which ensures the stability of the resulting sampling algorithm.

title: (A Variant of) Clifford Circuit Synthesis is NP-Complete
abstract: Optimal circuit synthesis is the problem of finding the shortest-depth circuit representation of a given functionality with respect to a pre-specified elementary gate set. This is a central problem in both quantum and classical hardware design. While the classical version is very well understood -- both in terms of heuristics and rigorous hardness assertions -- much less is known about optimal quantum circuit synthesis. We focus on optimal Clifford circuit synthesis, for which various heuristics are known, e.g. via reduction to 3-SAT. Our main result supplies a matching hardness result: a variant of optimal Clifford synthesis is NP-hard. The proof proceeds in two parts: (i) reduce 3-edge colorability on 3-regular graphs to a circuit synthesis problem that only involves CZ gates, (ii) prove that the availability of additional elementary Clifford gates -- most notably: Hadamard, phase and CNOT -- cannot lead to further improvements of the optimal circuit depth. Our work sharpens the complexity-theoretic understanding of Clifford circuits: simulation and equivalence checking are in P, whereas deciding whether a Clifford unitary admits an implementation within a prescribed depth is NP-complete.

title: Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI
abstract: Generative AI can support writing, but frictionless access may cause cognitive offloading before users develop their own ideas. We introduce Engage-to-Unlock, a productive-friction mechanism that unlocks generative capabilities after users meaningfully engage with the task. In a controlled experiment (N = 398), participants completed a writing task under one of four conditions: Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, Engage-to-Unlock, or Time-Matched Unlock, which matched unlock timing to Engage-to-Unlock participants but independent of users' engagement, then evaluated passages for evidence and inferential errors. Results show that Engage-to-Unlock redistributed effort across tasks: participants spent more time writing and less time evaluating, without increasing overall task duration. They also submitted more prompts than in other AI-assisted conditions and showed the highest accuracy-per-time evaluation efficiency across conditions. These findings suggest that designing GenAI access to encourage early human engagement may provide a productive form of friction, while retaining active AI use and efficient downstream evaluation.

evidence.title: Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI
evidence.abstract: Generative AI can support writing, but frictionless access may cause cognitive offloading before users develop their own ideas. We introduce Engage-to-Unlock, a productive-friction mechanism that unlocks generative capabilities after users meaningfully engage with the task. In a controlled experiment (N = 398), participants completed a writing task under one of four conditions: Human-Only, Standard Chatbot, Engage-to-Unlock, or Time-Matched Unlock, which matched unlock timing to Engage-to-Unlock participants but independent of users' engagement, then evaluated passages for evidence and inferential errors. Results show that Engage-to-Unlock redistributed effort across tasks: participants spent more time writing and less time evaluating, without increasing overall task duration. They also submitted more prompts than in other AI-assisted conditions and showed the highest accuracy-per-time evaluation efficiency across conditions. These findings suggest that designing GenAI access to encourage early human engagement may provide a productive form of friction, while retaining active AI use and efficient downstream evaluation.

title: Supervising Sound Localization by In-the-wild Egomotion
abstract: We present a method for learning binaural sound localization using egomotion as a supervisory signal. Over the course of a video, the cameras direction to a sound source will change as the camera moves. We train an audio model to predict sound directions that are consistent with visual estimates of camera motion, which we obtain using traditional methods from multi-view geometry. This provides a weak but plentiful form of supervision that we combine with traditional binaural cues. To evaluate this method, we propose a dataset of real-world audio-visual videos with egomotion. We show that our model can successfully learn from real-world data and that it performs well on sound localization tasks

title: From Steane to A7: Quantum Codes from Invariant States
abstract: We construct a two-parameter family of single-error-correcting seven-ququart codes with transversal $\tilde{A_7}$ symmetry, realizing the finite component of a two-qubit super-golden gate set. These $((7,4,3))_4$ codes encode two logical qubits and support non-Clifford operations by applying the same gate to each physical ququart. Our method constructs invariant parent states rather than searching directly for a codespace. For $n$ systems of local dimension $q$, suppose the local symmetry is a unitary $t$-group and the permutation symmetry is $t$-transitive. Maximal mixing of all marginals on at most $t$ sites is then equivalent to linear equations in Schur--Weyl sector weights. Every feasible solution yields parents of pure distance at least $t+1$; puncturing one site produces a $q$-dimensional code of distance at least $t$ with the prescribed local symmetry acting transversally. Steane and the nonstabilizer Fake Steane code reveal why the construction leaves continuous freedom. They share the same prescribed transversal Clifford and permutation symmetries, and their eight-qubit purifications lie on a circle: error correction fixes two invariant-sector norms but leaves the relative phase free. Keeping the same permutation group and replacing Clifford symmetry by $\tilde{A_7}$ $\leq SU(4)$ gives three fixed sector norms and two free relative phases, producing the new ququart family.

title: Mind the Gap: Continuous magnification sampling for pathology foundation models
abstract: In histopathology, pathologists examine both tissue architecture at low magnification and fine-grained morphology at high magnification. Yet, the performance of pathology foundation models across magnifications and the effect of magnification sampling during training remain poorly understood. We model magnification sampling as a multi-source domain adaptation problem and develop a simple theoretical framework that reveals systematic trade-offs between sampling strategies. We show that the widely used discrete uniform sampling of magnifications (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mpp) leads to degradation at intermediate magnifications. We introduce continuous magnification sampling, which removes gaps in magnification coverage while preserving performance at standard scales. Further, we derive sampling distributions that optimize representation quality across magnification scales. To evaluate these strategies, we introduce two new benchmarks (TCGA-MS, BRACS-MS) with appropriate metrics. Our experiments show that continuous sampling can improve downstream task performance at intermediate magnifications, with gains of up to 4 percentage points in balanced classification accuracy, and that optimized distributions can further improve performance. Finally, we evaluate current histopathology foundation models, finding that magnification is a primary driver of performance variation across models. Our work paves the way towards future pathology foundation models that perform reliably across magnifications.

title: RETHINKING AUTHORSHIP: A DOCTRINAL ANALYSIS OF COPYRIGHT PROTECTION FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-GENERATED WORKS
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence challenges a foundational assumption of copyright law: that protectable expression is attributable to a human author who exercises creative judgment.This article examines how copyright law should treat works generated or materially assisted by AI, with particular attention to authorship, originality, ownership, and the threshold of human creative contribution.Using a comparative doctrinal method, it analyses statutory provisions, judicial decisions, administrative practice, and ongoing reform initiatives in the United States, United Kingdom, European Union, and India.The analysis considers, inter alia, Thaler v. Perlmutter and U.S. Copyright Office guidance; section 9(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 and the United Kingdom's reform debate; the Court of Justice of the European Union's "author's own intellectual creation" jurisprudence and the transparency framework under Article 53 of the EU AI Act; and India's section 2(d) of the Copyright Act, 1957 together with the RAGHAV/Suryast registration episode.The comparison reveals substantial convergence around the need for identifiable human creative input, notwithstanding significant differences in legal technique and the continued existence of statutory provisions for computer-generated works in the United Kingdom and India.The principal unresolved question is not whether human contribution matters, but how much creative control, selection, arrangement, modification, or other expressive intervention is sufficient to support authorship in AI-assisted works.The article argues that neither categorical exclusion nor unrestricted protection adequately addresses this intermediate zone.It therefore proposes a disclosure-based rebuttable presumption under which claimants identify the nature and extent of AI 1 5th-Semester B.A. LL.B. title: Meaning in the Reader: How Language Models Assemble Scientific Assessments:Factor-Specific Signals, Local Semantic Binding, and Interface-Dependent Readout
abstract: When a language model assesses a scientific result, it is natural to imagine that it first forms stable internal variables–for example, how well established the result is and how consequential it would be if true–and then reads those variables out into a report. We find a more layered and reader-dependent computation. First, an orthogonal seven-factor study varies raw evidence, methodological quality, replication, verification, prior plausibility, conditional consequence, and target relevance. Structured reports preserve all seven directed factor effects on held-out scenes, ruling out a simple account in which complete scientific assessment is exhausted by two fixed report variables. Second, low-dimensional hidden geometry is nevertheless real: a nuisance-controlled late assessment span is stable within its source population, while new evidence/consequence coordinates systematically rotate across reordered, paraphrased, and free-form interfaces. Third, exact-state interventions identify a clause-local causal assessment signal. Consequence-associated perturbations transfer across scenes and paraphrases, but their semantic field is not self-contained in the donor state. A perturbation derived from another factor can produce nearly the same consequence effect when inserted into the recipient consequence slot, whereas the same consequence perturbation is much weaker when inserted into a different slot. The donor directions themselves are only moderately aligned. These results support a reader-assigned assessment computation: upstream states preserve factor-sensitive signals and partially portable signed/value components; the recipient slot and local reader assign much of the field semantics; and the report interface determines how these components are mixed and amplified into settlement, consequence, verification, relevance, and other outputs. The earlier low-dimensional assessment geometry is therefore better understood as a reader-specific pooled summary than as a universal fixed semantic coordinate system. Scientific judgement in language models is not simply stored and then reported; it is assembled at readout

title: Sentiment Analysis Using Large Language Models : A Review
abstract: Sentiment analysis is an important Natural Language Processing (NLP) task for identifying opinions, attitudes, and emotional polarity in user-generated text.Recent research has examined Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, GPT-4, LLaMA, and related models for zero-shot, few-shot, prompt-based, multilingual, and aspectbased sentiment analysis.Compared with conventional supervised approaches, LLMs provide flexible naturallanguage task formulation, but published studies also report challenges related to consistency, domain adaptation, multilingual performance, fine-grained classification, sarcasm, explainability, and computational cost This paper presents a review of sentiment analysis using Large Language Models, with particular attention to user reviews and the analysis of generative-AI applications.The review covers traditional feature-based methods, LLM prompting and classification approaches, multilingual and aspect-based sentiment analysis, and application-oriented review mining.A five-class sentiment frameworkvery negative, negative, neutral, positive, and very positiveis considered as a fine-grained alternative to binary classification.The review further identifies research gaps involving binary-class limitations, dataset size and diversity, domain adaptation, and reliable evaluation.These observations motivate the proposed study of Google Gemini mobile-application reviews using TF-IDF and machinelearning classifiers, with evaluation through Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score.

title: Verification Companion for the Revised Orthogonal-Circle Ruled Surface v5
abstract: Verification companion to Akari Hayami (Jian-Yu Huang), The Orthogonal-Circle Ruled Surface: A Boundary Atlas, Five Rank Singularities, and Conditional Fold-Signal Recurrence (v5; paper DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23073642). New in version 0.04 (research beyond the published article): the global self-intersection is classified. On the closed parameter rectangle, distinct labels of S(t,u) = (c + 2u(1-c), (1-u) sin t, u sqrt(c(2-c))), c = cos t, share an image exactly on the u = 1 seam or on two mirror double arcs. Each arc's source closure runs from the edge label (±π/2, 2/5) through the interior cross-cap to the base label (±arccos(4/5), 0); the common image starts at (4/5, ±3/5, 0). The quotient double curve has an explicit rational parametrization, and the squared eliminant requires a retained sign condition. Lean (RuledV5/SelfIntersection.lean, DoubleFamily.lean, DoubleNormalization.lean; 22 new theorems) proves, for the actual surface: the seam criterion, mirror-half separation, the exact boundary double points, the universal elimination certificate, sufficiency of the explicit family for every 0 ≤ v < √5 - 2 with its actual image, and the converse in each open angular half (two distinct labels with equal images are exactly the explicit pair for a unique v). The closed-rectangle assembly, global two-label bound, cross-cap singleton fibers, smoothness of the source arcs and the quotient homeomorphism are written proofs in papers/legacy-geometry/orthogonal-circle-ruled-surface/notes/SELF_INTERSECTION.md. The exceptional germ is classified in the Stokes caustic v5 Lean companion v0.05 (10.5281/zenodo.23422752). All 246 public named RuledV5 theorems (224 in v0.03) and the 268 StokesV5 dependency theorems pass build, status, an exhaustive axiom audit (only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) and a proof-hole scan; the two inventories are separate. The article as a whole is not Lean-formalized; see companions/lean/ruled-surface-v5/COVERAGE.md. The deposit contains the sealed source-only ZIP (SHA-256 7c738d9b1bdb9e2073dea6ffafee7b2b0d0909d7aa2e48a0c7240a13f1a6508d), which includes the StokesV5 dependency so it builds on its own, and its receipt; run python3 -B verify.py inside the package. Repository release: https://github.com/Akari-H-111/hayami-mathematical-research/releases/tag/ruled-surface-v5-companion-v0.04. Cite the article and this software version separately; the concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23073653 identifies all versions. Earlier versions are unchanged. Code: Apache-2.0. Documentation, notes and figures: CC-BY-4.0.

title: Computational data for projective Steenrod--Milnor codes over $\mathbb{F}_4$
abstract: Exact computational data supporting Appendices A and B of the manuscript on projective Steenrod--Milnor codes over $\mathbb{F}_4$. The archive contains finite-field matrices, Hermitian dual and hull data, weight distributions, relative CSS distance certificates, binary and higher-dimensional computations, and explicit socket permutations for the Tanner constituents. Reproducible Python verification programs and their generated certificates are included.

title: CGAT-PAD: A Consistency-Guided Anomaly Transformer for Photovoltaic Anomaly Detection
abstract: With the large-scale deployment of photovoltaic (PV) systems, time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) in PV operation data has become important for maintaining operational safety and energy yield. In practical PV scenarios, anomaly labels are scarce, and unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) methods are often affected by low-quality training data and insufficient modeling of multivariate physical coupling. To address these challenges, this paper proposes the Consistency-Guided Anomaly Transformer for Photovoltaic Anomaly Detection (CGAT-PAD). The Tri-domain Consistency Assessment Module (TCAM) evaluates training-sample quality in the time, frequency, and residual domains, using physically grouped synchronous perturbation augmentation to support the generation of a consistency index. The Consistency-Guided Anomaly Transformer (CGAT) then incorporates this index into the Anomaly Transformer (AT) training loss as an adaptive weight, thereby down-weighting low-quality samples while retaining useful normal patterns. A controlled evaluation benchmark is constructed from real Photovoltaic Data Acquisition (PVDAQ) operation records by injecting reproducible synthetic anomalies into the test segment. Evaluation using F1, F1 PA%K , and AUC shows that CGAT-PAD outperforms the compared baselines, indicating the value of tri-domain consistency guidance for robust detection in nonstationary PV data.

title: The accuracy–utility gap: Why AI accuracy does not guarantee clinical benefit in digital pathology
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in digital pathology has repeatedly achieved expert-level diagnostic accuracy under controlled validation conditions. However, its clinical translation—reflected in regulatory approval, routine adoption, changes in diagnostic decisions, or demonstrated patient benefit—remains inconsistent. This viewpoint argues that this discrepancy arises because diagnostic accuracy is a property of a model under specified conditions, whereas clinical utility emerges from the entire sociotechnical pathway in which the model is deployed. Building on recent work on standardization, system selection, institutional validation, and trial governance, we integrate these complementary layers into a continuous tissue-to-outcome pathway comprising six stages: tissue, image, model, workflow, decision, and outcome, with each stage explicitly linked to the claim it can support. Variability introduced at any stage may remain undetected and propagate downstream, potentially affecting clinical decisions and patient care. Accordingly, evidence generated at one stage cannot substitute for that required to support claims at subsequent stages. We therefore propose a stage-linked evidence map that identifies the principal risk and evidence required at each stage, while making explicit which stronger downstream claims remain unsupported. This framework enables reviewers and institutions considering adoption to identify where a study has addressed the accuracy–utility gap and where uncertainty remains. Evaluating AI across the complete pathway reframes the evidentiary requirements for clinical translation: high diagnostic accuracy is necessary, but insufficient, to establish meaningful clinical utility.

title: Exploring the risks of generative AI misuse via ambiguous prompts: Bypassing safety filters in Text-to-Image/Video models
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) has introduced new textual and multimedia data generation capabilities. Recently, several new Text-to-Image/Video (T2I/V) models have been released, demonstrating advanced capabilities in generating realistic images and video from textual prompts. These models have been conceived to maximize their usability across a broad audience, ensuring that users with varying levels of domain expertise can easily interact with them. However, many of these models often fail to meet comprehensive safety criteria, leaving significant gaps in their ability to prevent the generation of unethical or harmful content. This lack of robust safeguards increases the risk that such tools may be misused, intentionally or unintentionally, to produce media that violates ethical standards or propagates misinformation. This research explores the ethical implications of emerging T2I/V models by investigating their ability to generate unethical multimedia content, such as that containing stereotypes, prejudice, violence, and discrimination. To this end, we employ ambiguous prompts, which are seemingly benign or neutral prompts but can be crafted by domain-expert users to bypass the models’ safety mechanisms and indirectly provoke the generation of harmful content. Through user analysis and the evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) like Claude and Gemini, we find that, while many T2I/V models are designed to avoid generating unethical content, they still produce a significant amount of discriminatory and stereotypical media. A complementary user study involving 50 participants further shows that such content is widely perceived as offensive, non-inclusive, and unsuitable for younger or vulnerable audiences. Conversely, the results demonstrate that Claude Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro show a moderate but promising capacity to analyze and identify unethical elements within multimedia content.

However, many of these models often fail to meet comprehensive safety criteria, leaving significant gaps in their ability to prevent the generation of unethical or harmful content. This lack of robust safeguards increases the risk that such tools may be misused, intentionally or unintentionally, to produce media that violates ethical standards or propagates misinformation. This research explores the ethical implications of emerging T2I/V models by investigating their ability to generate unethical multimedia content, such as that containing stereotypes, prejudice, violence, and discrimination. To this end, we employ ambiguous prompts, which are seemingly benign or neutral prompts but can be crafted by domain-expert users to bypass the models’ safety mechanisms and indirectly provoke the generation of harmful content. Through user analysis and the evaluation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) like Claude and Gemini, we find that, while many T2I/V models are designed to avoid generating unethical content, they still produce a significant amount of discriminatory and stereotypical media. A complementary user study involving 50 participants further shows that such content is widely perceived as offensive, non-inclusive, and unsuitable for younger or vulnerable audiences. Conversely, the results demonstrate that Claude Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro show a moderate but promising capacity to analyze and identify unethical elements within multimedia content.

title: Bandits via Additive Quantized Representations
abstract: Contextual bandits require balancing nonlinear reward modeling with online efficiency. Tree ensembles and neural methods capture nonlinearities but require periodic retraining and large replay buffers. Linear models update efficiently per observation with O(1) memory, but are fundamentally restricted to linear reward structures. We propose Residual Quantization (RQ) as a representation layer to bridge this gap. An offline-trained RQ codebook maps continuous contexts into discrete centroid assignments across multiple levels, set dynamically through a shadow mechanism. This enables a spectrum of additive bandit algorithms that achieve nonlinear expressivity with strictly bounded memory. Across 13 datasets, RQ variants beat their non-RQ counterparts on 11 of 13 datasets, often by wide margins, while matching doubling-retrain XGBoost and neural baselines using up to 1000 times less memory.

title: Stochastic Rounding in Low-Precision Transformer Inference: A Variable-Precision Emulation Study of a Small GPT-2
abstract: Should low-precision transformer inference use stochastic rounding (SR) or round-to-nearest (RN)? The answer depends on where in the network you look. We isolate this effect by holding the numerical format fixed and varying only the rounding rule at individual operation sites. To enable experiments at freely chosen precisions, we extend the PRISM vectorized rounding library to arbitrary virtual precision via a variable-precision stochastic rounding (VPSR) algorithm, proving that the rounding decision is evaluated exactly in hardware floating point. We develop two analyses providing complementary insight into this site-level trade-off. First, a probabilistic forward-error bound for linear projections shows that SR's error envelope grows as $O(\sqrt{n} u)$ in reduction length $n$, versus $O(n u)$ for RN, a gap that widens rapidly at low precision and is most pronounced in the long multilayer perceptron (MLP) down-projection. Second, a second-order decomposition of expected cross-entropy loss change at the output softmax into signed drift, drift curvature, and a Fisher-weighted variance penalty reveals why the two sites behave oppositely: MLP noise is predominantly a uniform logit shift to which softmax is invariant, so SR's variance is largely discounted; head noise is non-uniform across the vocabulary and is not. On DistilGPT-2 at $t=6$ significand bits, observations match theory: SR in the MLP raises perplexity to 1.15x the full-precision reference, versus 2.21x for RN. At the language-model head, the ordering reverses because SR introduces non-uniform variance, whereas deterministic RN carries none. In a mixed-precision configuration (MLP output at $t=6$), assigning SR to the MLP and RN to the head brings perplexity within 1.10x of the full-precision reference, a 28% reduction over matched-bit RN.

title: Unflattening by Flattening -- How Input Distributions Shape Output Variance in Angle-Encoded Circuits
abstract: Barren plateaus hinder training of parameterized quantum circuits by making loss gradients exponentially small in the number of qubits. For angle-encoded product states, we show how the input distribution affects output variation through algebraic input purity, i.e. the input's overlap with the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra. With the specified readouts and Haar or exact group 2-design sampling, matchgate circuits on $n$ qubits retain output variance of order $1/n$ for every pure product input. The off-diagonal family instead has zero output on computational-basis inputs at any depth and for every parameter choice. Independent uniform angles yield mean variance of the same order as matchgates. A count of diagonal Pauli strings identifies these zero-output endpoints. For any fixed dataset of nonzero inputs with at least $2n$ coordinates, we construct a classical preprocessing certificate. A shared random rotation is accepted only when the dataset's mean purity passes a computable threshold. This certifies mean output variance of order $1/n$ for the off-diagonal family before circuit execution, with a constant expected number of trials. Binary and ternary weighted encodings also recover the independent-angle mean purity from one uniform scalar input. Numerical experiments examine training behavior and extensions to larger algebras. The guarantee concerns output variance averaged over inputs, while successful learning also depends on the task and information preserved by the encoding.

title: Is it Possible to Generate Irreversible PolyProtected Templates from Face Embeddings using System-Specific Keys?
abstract: This work aims to answer the question of whether it is possible to generate irreversible protected templates when the PolyProtect biometric template protection method is applied to face embeddings using system-specific keys (i.e., the same C and E parameters, which define the transform, are applied to all subjects' face embeddings), instead of the traditional subject-specific keys (i.e., each subject has their own C and E parameters). This is important for determining whether we can perform de-duplication of face identities in the PolyProtected domain, which is not possible in the subject-specific key scenario due to the clash with PolyProtect's unlinkability property (i.e., one could generate multiple protected templates belonging to the same identity, using different C and E parameters, such that those templates cannot be linked to each other). We present experiments (reproducible using our open-source code) to prove that there exist at least three ways of systematically selecting system-specific keys that produce irreversible PolyProtected templates: (i) from pre-selected subject-specific keys, (ii) by applying a previously proposed key selection algorithm to random vectors, and (iii) by approximating a "good" C/E pair distribution from which system-specific keys can be constructed. Our findings thus point to the conclusion that it is, indeed, possible to safely operate PolyProtect in the system-specific key scenario without degrading the template protection potential. This opens up the possibility for identity de-duplication in the PolyProtected domain.

title: Unitary fault-tolerant encoding of Pauli states in surface codes
abstract: In fault-tolerant quantum computation, the preparation of logical states is a ubiquitous subroutine, yet significant challenges persist even for the simplest states required. In the present work, we present a unitary, scalable, distance-preserving encoding scheme for preparing Pauli eigenstates in surface codes. Unlike previous unitary approaches whose fault-distance remains constant with increasing code distance, our scheme ensures that the protection offered by the code is preserved during state preparation. Building on strategies discovered by reinforcement learning for the surface-17 code, we generalize the construction to arbitrary code distances and both rotated and unrotated surface codes. The proposed encoding relies only on geometrically local gates, and is therefore fully compatible with planar 2D qubit connectivity, and it achieves circuit depth scaling as O ( d ), consistent with fundamental entanglement-generation bounds. We design explicit stabilizer-expanding circuits with and without ancilla-mediated connectivity and analyze their error-propagation behavior. Numerical simulations under depolarizing noise show that our unitary encoding without ancillas outperforms standard stabilizer-measurement-based schemes, reducing logical error rates by up to an order of magnitude. These results make the scheme particularly relevant for platforms such as trapped ions and neutral atoms, where measurements are costly relative to gates and idling noise is considerably weaker than gate noise. Our work bridges the gap between measurement-based and unitary encodings of surface-code states and opens new directions for distance-preserving state preparation in fault-tolerant quantum computation.

title: RS-2026-083 - Why We Built Our Own: Design Rationale for a From-Scratch Agentic AI Security Control Plane
abstract: Agent frameworks have become critical infrastructure, yet they were not designed as security boundaries. This paper documents the design rationale for a from-scratch agentic AI security control plane built independently of any third-party agent framework. We present the requirements that forced the build, the architecture that resulted, and seven months of production operation across 50+ security modules across 17 verticals. We position our work against prior art — OATS, LICITRA-SENTRY, DROS-6P, Ring Zero, and AgentWard — and identify the gap: a production-tested implementation that owns cryptographic evidence chains, native action gating, and a runtime kill switch within a single architecture.

title: Confidence-Aware Autonomous Knowledge Graph Evolution for Lifelong Robotic TAMP Systems
abstract: Neuro-symbolic Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) architectures anchor Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning within a Knowledge Graph (KG) K to eliminate plan-level hallucinations, but letting K evolve autonomously across missions risks contaminating it with confidently-wrong facts that both the planner and the perception stack will then trust. We formalize this problem and address it with a unified Autonomous Knowledge Update framework combining confidence-aware entity-attribute belief fusion, geolocated obstacle ingestion, and density-based emergence of Zones of Interest, all governed by the same hybrid syntactic-semantic Dempster-Shafer fusion rule so that contamination resistance is a property of the framework ratherthan of any single channel. We give a full algorithmic specification of its three update channels and a field evaluation over 8-mission made in a EU H2020 OLGA project context deployment that shows obstacle-driven mid-mission replanning triggers falling from 10 to 0 events, KG growth correlating with plan richness at r = 0.993, our fusion mechanism keeping contamination roughly an order of magnitude lower than a naive last-write-wins updater across tested observation error rates, and cross-checking the on-board recognition module against K raising its top-1 accuracy from 89.7% to 94.0% over the campaign.

title: Generative AI in Fashion E-Commerce Product Imagery: An Experimental Test of Image Origin and Transparency Labelling on Consumer Trust, Perceived Product Quality and Purchase Intention
abstract: Retailers are increasingly replacing photographic model shoots with synthetic product imagery generated by text-to-image systems, a deployment decision that couples substantial production savings with an unresolved question about consumer response and about the transparency obligations attached to synthetic content. This study examines how AI-generated and photographic product images are evaluated in fashion e-commerce and how a visible origin label affects that evaluation. A 2 (image origin: AI-generated vs. photograph) × 2 (labelling: absent vs. present) between-subjects online experiment was conducted with 150 participants. Consumer trust, perceived product quality and purchase intention were measured with established scales, and general attitude toward artificial intelligence was tested as a moderator. Without labelling, no statistically significant differences between the two image types emerged on any dependent variable. The visible label reduced perceived product quality significantly but modestly, while effects on trust and purchase intention, the image origin by label interaction and moderation were not statistically significant.

title: Corpus Poisoning Method for RAG Systems Based on Monte Carlo Tree Search
authors: LI Bohan, CAI Manchun, ZHANG Teng
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems enhance the timeliness and factual consistency of large language models (LLMs) by incorporating an external knowledge base. However, this structure also makes them highly vulnerable to corpus poisoning attacks, particularly in black-box scenarios where internal model parameters are inaccessible. To address the challenge of constructing adversarial passages that can approximate target queries in the embedding space under black-box conditions, this paper proposes an attack framework for RAG corpus poisoning based on structured search. Specifically, the framework models the adversarial sample construction as a high-dimensional combinatorial optimization problem in the discrete text space. It introduces Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) to enable global planning of candidate token sequences and leverages a dynamic vocabulary generated by GPT-4o to enhance the search??s semantic relevance and efficiency. The resulting adversarial passage is then injected into the knowledge base and iteratively refined through validation, achieving stable retrieval hijacking in a black-box setting. Systemic experiments on multiple benchmark datasets and various sizes of Qwen2.5 models demonstrate the robust attack performance of the proposed framework, achieving an average retrieval hijack status at Rank 1 of 89.0% and a final answer contamination status of 83.9%. Experimental results demonstrate that, without requiring gradient information or access to internal model parameters, the proposed method effectively optimizes retrieval ranking signals through structured search, achieving higher attack success rates and better stealthiness than existing heuristic-based approaches.

title: Assessment of Global Horizontal Irradiance Data Quality and Calibration Uncertainty in a Tropical Monsoon Region: A Case Study in Kamphaeng Phet, Thailand
abstract: Ground-based solar radiation data are useful for environmental studies and solar-energy assessment, especially in tropical monsoon regions where sky conditions change throughout the year. This study investigated the quality and variability of hourly global horizontal irradiance (GHI) measured at Kamphaeng Phet Rajabhat University, Thailand, from January to December 2025. GHI was measured using an SMP10-V thermopile pyranometer. The instrument recorded data every 5 s, and the data were later averaged into hourly values. The dataset was checked by separating daylight hours, assessing data availability, and applying preliminary physical range screening. Nighttime periods were not treated as missing data, and no gap filling was performed. During the study period, 4,420 daylight hourly records were expected. Of these, 4,355 records were available and passed the physical range screening, giving an overall daylight-data availability of 98.53%. The record-weighted annual mean hourly GHI was 404.63 W/m2. Monthly mean GHI ranged from 322.50 W/m2 in July to 474.36 W/m2 in March. The seasonal results showed that mean GHI was highest in summer and lowest in the rainy season. The rainy season also showed the highest relative variability because atmospheric conditions were more variable during this period. The pyranometer calibration certificate reported an expanded calibration uncertainty of 1.39% at k=2. These results provide a local reference for measured GHI characteristics and data-quality evaluation in a tropical monsoon environment.

title: The Choose-Your-Own-Adventure Calculus
abstract: In many programming systems, the user can interactively construct a program by repeatedly triggering a completion mechanism and choosing one of the offered options. This is the case with code editors for object-oriented languages (choosing a member), data exploration environments (choosing a transformation), but also with theorem provers (choosing a tactic) and structure editors (choosing a grammar~rule).

title: A Generative Model of Complex Networks Using Graphons and Neural Inverse Operators
abstract: Generative graph models are central to understanding and simulating complex networks. However, existing approaches have complementary strengths and limitations. Mechanistic models offer interpretability but rely on instance-specific estimation methods. Deep generative models, on the other hand, offer amortized inference at the cost of interpretability and are largely limited to graph sizes seen during training. Scientific applications motivate a framework that retains the strengths of both paradigms. We bridge them by formulating both the generative model and parameter recovery in function space. A multifractal step graphon extends standard step graphons with a recursive construction that compactly parameterizes complex networks. This formulation admits a neural inverse operator to recover its parameters, enabling inference on unseen graph sizes. We evaluate our model, trained only on synthetic multifractal step graphon realizations, against both paradigms. Against a graph foundation model pretrained on empirical networks, our method achieves the best average performance on three of four metrics in a zero-shot graph-generation benchmark, indicating that the model transfers to real-world graphs. We also apply our method to single-observation networks, a regime largely inaccessible to deep models that require training corpora, where it performs comparably to an instance-specific method that optimizes on each graph. In a multi-subject EEG case study, the inferred parameters track a reversible change in brain state more sensitively than traditional network statistics. Together, these results indicate that mechanistic interpretability and amortized inference can be effectively unified in a generative graph model to enhance our understanding of complex networks.

In a multi-subject EEG case study, the inferred parameters track a reversible change in brain state more sensitively than traditional network statistics. Together, these results indicate that mechanistic interpretability and amortized inference can be effectively unified in a generative graph model to enhance our understanding of complex networks.

title: TRACE: Tackling Real-World Resource Assignment Problems via Agentic Heuristic Design
abstract: Dynamic resource assignment, the real-time allocation of task streams to heterogeneous processing nodes, is the backbone of modern computing infrastructure. While learning-based schedulers excel in research, industrial deployments still rely on hand-written rules that operators can read, audit, and execute within tight latency budgets. LLM-based Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD) promises to automate writing such rules. However, existing AHD frameworks were developed for combinatorial problems fully specified to the LLM, and they learn only from a scalar fitness score. In real systems, the behaviour that determines a good heuristic, such as processor speeds or power consumption, is unknown a priori: the score reveals which heuristic performs better, but not why. This missing information is recorded in the system logs that every evaluation produces. Exploiting it is non-trivial: logs are massive and noisy, the relevant signals depend on the objective, and their content and format vary across hardware and software stacks, so they can neither be fed to an LLM as is nor processed by a fixed parser. We propose TRACE, which couples an evolutionary AHD loop with an agentic knowledge-extraction workflow. A Reasoner agent analyzes the log schema in light of the objective and formulates hypotheses about the system dynamics; a Coder agent writes and executes schema-specific code to test them, producing insights or executable tools for the evolved heuristics. We evaluate TRACE on a synthetic cloud benchmark and a 5G vRAN scenario built from industrial testbed measurements and operational traffic traces. TRACE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art AHD methods in resource assignment problems and yields more auditable heuristics at under 2% overhead.

title: Towards Retrieval Augmented Generation in High-Energy and Astroparticle Physics
abstract: The high-energy and astroparticle physics literature has grown into an enormous body of knowledge. Gaining a comprehensive understanding of this literature is an important step in research, but is a challenging task. Before making meaningful advances, it is important to establish what has already been done and identify open questions. However, this process is becoming increasingly difficult given the sheer volume of publications. Conducting a focused literature survey on a narrow topic is particularly challenging. We develop an open-source Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline to produce concise, targeted summary reports with citations, grounded in the database of arXiv papers, enabling researchers, editors, and referees to rapidly orient themselves within any corner of the field. Specifically, we embed approximately 230K hep-ph and astro-ph.HE papers to enable a hybrid retrieval that captures both keyword matches and semantic similarity. The fused candidate set is then refined using a cross-encoder reranker. Following retrieval, the papers are passed to a Large Language Model (LLM), for which we use Google DeepMind's open-source Gemma-4-E4B model. The LLM first acts as a judge to evaluate the relevance and then synthesizes a coherent and grounded report with references. This modern AI-driven approach allows us to go beyond the capabilities of classical keyword search on arXiv or Inspire-HEP.

title: Universal Dilation of Linear Itô SDEs: Quantum Trajectories and Lindblad Simulation of Second Moments
abstract: We present a universal framework for simulating N -dimensional linear Itô stochastic differential equations (SDEs) on quantum computers with additive or multiplicative noises. Building on a unitary dilation technique, we establish a rigorous mapping from the general linear SDEs d X t = A ( t ) X t d t + ∑ j = 1 J B j ( t ) X t d W t j to stochastic Schrödinger equations (SSE) on a dilated Hilbert space. Crucially, this embedding is pathwise exact in that the classical solution is recovered as a projection of the dilated quantum state for each fixed noise realization. We demonstrate that the resulting SSEs are naturally implementable on digital quantum processors, where the stochastic Wiener increments are encoded directly by preparing the ancillary qubits. Exploiting this physical mapping, we develop two algorithmic strategies: (1) a trajectory-based approach that uses sequential weak measurements to realize efficient stochastic integrators, including a second-order scheme, and (2) an ensemble-based approach that maps moment evolution to a deterministic Lindblad quantum master equation, enabling simulation without Monte Carlo sampling. We provide error bounds based on a stochastic light-cone analysis and validate the framework with numerical experiments.

title: الابتكار في البحث العلمي المدعوم بالذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيل: الاتجاهات والتطبيقات والتحديات الناشئة
abstract: يتناول البحث الابتكار في البحث العلمي المدعوم بالذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيل، في ضوء الانتقال من استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي بوصفه أداة مساعدة إلى أنظمة قادرة على التخطيط، واستخدام الأدوات، وتنفيذ مهام بحثية مترابطة بدرجات متفاوتة من الاستقلالية. ويهدف إلى تأصيل مفهوم الذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيل، وتحليل تطبيقاته في مراحل البحث العلمي، وبيان أبرز تحدياته المنهجية والعلمية والحوكمية. واعتمد البحث المنهج الوصفي التحليلي من خلال مراجعة الأدبيات العلمية الحديثة ذات الصلة وتحليل اتجاهاتها وتطبيقاتها. وأظهرت النتائج أن الذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيل يختلف عن الاستخدام التقليدي للذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي بقدرته على إدارة مهام متعددة نحو هدف محدد، وأن تطبيقاته تمتد من توليد الأفكار والفرضيات إلى الاكتشاف والتحليل العلمي والتجريب المؤتمت والمختبرات ذاتية القيادة. كما تبين أن زيادة استقلالية هذه الأنظمة ترافقها تحديات تتعلق بدقة المخرجات، وانتقال الأخطاء بين مراحل التنفيذ، وقابلية التتبع والتحقق، والنزاهة العلمية، وتحديد المسؤولية. وخلص البحث إلى أن القيمة الحقيقية للذكاء الاصطناعي الوكيل لا تكمن في استبدال الباحث، بل في إعادة تنظيم سير العمل البحثي ضمن تكامل منضبط بين القدرات الوكيلية والحكم العلمي البشري. ويوصي البحث بالتحقق البشري من المراحل الجوهرية، وتوثيق استخدام الأنظمة الوكيلية، وتقييم العملية البحثية كاملة، وتحديد مستويات واضحة لتفويض المهام وفق طبيعتها ومخاطرها. كما يدعو إلى دراسات تقارن أداء الباحث والنظام الوكيلي والعمل المشترك بينهما في مراحل البحث المختلفة.

title: Mitigating Cascading Prompt Injections in Multi-Agent Systems via Semantic Boundary Mediation and Observability
abstract: The rapid industrial adoption of autonomous agentic workflows on cloud-native platforms has shifted the primary cybersecurity attack surface from model-layer alignment to system-layer execution privileges. This research identifies and analyses the emerging threat of Cascading Prompt Injections (CPI) within multi-agent systems (MAS). In a CPI scenario, a compromised or manipulated “Supervisor Agent” propagates malicious, high-privilege instructions to downstream “Worker Agents” that possess broad execution scopes, bypassing traditional input-layer guardrails. We demonstrate that existing safety filters are ineffective against these inter-agent escalations due to the “Confused Deputy” vulnerability inherent in default service account configurations. To address this, we introduce the Semantic Boundary Framework (SBF), a zero-trust architectural mediation layer implemented on Google Cloud Platform (GCP). The SBF utilizes an event-driven verification proxy to measure “Intent Drift” between the user’s original prompt and the resulting worker-level API calls. By applying geometric vector analysis via Vertex AI Vector Search, the framework mathematically validates the congruency of agentic actions in real-time. Experimental results using a three-tier swarm on Vertex AI show a 74% increase in the detection of cross-agent privilege escalation while introducing a negligible mean latency of 58ms. This paper provides a scalable roadmap to implement semantic-aware security in autonomous cloud ecosystems without sacrificing operational performance.

title: Data from Radiometer (RAD) measurements at Paris – Chemin Vert Bobigny (PACHEM) from 2023-06-29 to 2024-03-04 [L0]
abstract: Combined and uncalibrated logger data from radiometer measurements on a sun tracker with global, direct and diffuse shortwave irradiance and longwave irradiance at Paris – Chemin Vert Bobigny (PACHEM) (Département 93) in the urbanized area in the NE of Greater Paris recorded during the urbisphere Paris Campaign from 2023-06-29 00:00 to 2024-03-05 00:00 UTC. Measuerments were taken at roof level on top of a residential high-rise buiding at 48.904672°N / 2.4447328°E. The L0 datafile combines all individual uncalibrated logger files (automatic transfer, manual download) with a consistent and consecutive time axis. Missing data is filled with -9999. The data file has each time step as a row and each parameter as a column in comma-separated csv format. The columns contain readings converted to physical units with simple quality control from all radiometers and a co-located all-in one automatic weather station (AWS). The file PACHEM-MET_1min-202306290000_202403050000_UTC.csv has the format of a comma-separated .csv file with 4 header lines following the Campbell Scientific Inc. TOA5 file definition. The L0 data combined all raw data files into a single .csv file covering the entire period of observations at PAAUNA from 2023-06-29 00:00 to 2024-03-05 11:03 UTC based on RAW data averaged every minute. RAW data (individual logger output files) can be found here: Morrison, W., Hilland, R., Looschelders, D., Zeeman, M., Grimmond, S., & Christen, A. (2024). Data from Radiometer (RAD) measurements at Paris – Chemin Vert Bobigny (PACHEM) from 2023-06-28 to 2024-03-04 [RAW] (Version v1.0.2) [Dataset]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.12967485 Radiation measurements taken at PACHEM are: Direct normal irradiance (DNI) with an CHP1 pyrheliometer Global (solar) hemispherical irradiance (GHI) with an actively ventilated Kipp&Zonen CM21 pyranometer Diffuse (solar) irradiance with an actively ventilated and shaded Kipp&Zonen CM21 pyranometer Longwave hemispherical irradiance (LHI) with an actively ventilated and shaded Kipp&Zonen CG1 pyrgeometer All radiation fluxes are measured using a sun tracker (Kipp & Zonen SOLYS2) and continuously ventilated instruments. Further, the dataset contains simple meteorological measurements of barometric pressure, wind velocity, wind direction, air temperature, humidity, precipitation and lightning using a all-in-one weather station (Campbell Scientific ClimaVue 50) installed next to the sun tracker. The dataset is calibrated using manufacturer calibrations for all instruments and no further quality controlls or gap filling procedures have been applied. For quality controlled and calibrated data use L2 data instead. title: SentryLine: Reviewable Capability Traces for CPython Plugin Hosts
abstract: SentryLine makes CPython plugin admission explainable at the boundary. The host declares which authority a plugin may exercise; SentryLine records attempted authority classes and reports or rejects the first forbidden prefix before the instrumented effect is allowed to proceed. In the packaged evaluation, the combined monitor preserves all 28 benign workloads, blocks all 72 misuse workloads, and checks 13,888 boundary decisions with zero independent-contract disagreements and zero witnessless rejections. Audit-only monitoring blocks 38 of 72 misuse workloads, which is why the poster shows both interpreter-side and wrapper-side evidence. SentryLine is an admission-time review tool, not a universal Python sandbox.
